scope: Primary sources for tethered-wing control and biological sailors; winds are committed project products named in sailing.py INPUT_FILES.

sources.citation: Aaron, K. M., Heun, M. K. and Nock, K. T. (2002). A method for balloon trajectory control. Advances in Space Research 30(5), 1227-1232.
sources.access: Full text of the authors' draft (COSPAR 2000 paper) read by a verification agent; published abstract seen as an index snippet.
sources.use: A wing on a tether up to 15 km below a stratospheric balloon gives the drift a bias velocity of a few m/s; the balloon acts as the keel and the wing as the sail; example zonal wind differences of 26 m/s (Alice Springs, January) and 11 m/s (Fairbanks, July) between 35 and 20 km; a 100-day simulation with a 5 m2 wing.
sources.limit: Concept with simulations and a 1999 quarter-scale tether test; no flight measurement of drift; no lift coefficient or tether-drag analysis in the draft.

sources.citation: Iosilevskii, G. and Weihs, D. (2009). Hydrodynamics of sailing of the Portuguese man-of-war Physalia physalis. Journal of the Royal Society Interface 6(36), 613-626.
sources.access: PubMed abstract and PMC full-text passages (Introduction, sections 3.1, 3.3, 5, Appendix A, Conclusions) read by a verification agent.
sources.use: Aerodynamic forces on the float balance hydrodynamic forces on tentacles and polyps; largest angle from downwind 50-55 degrees at angle of attack 15-20 degrees; about 40-45 degrees at 40 degrees attack, as Totton and Mackie (1960) reported; sailing speed a few tens of cm/s, maximum about 0.4 m/s; mirror forms sail on opposite tacks.

sources.citation: Francis, L. (1991). Sailing downwind: aerodynamic performance of the Velella sail. Journal of Experimental Biology 158, 117-132.
sources.use: Low aspect ratio, flat-polar, primarily drag-based sail; maximum force at attack angles of 50-90 degrees; free sailors at 28-87 degrees with hulls broadside to the apparent water flow; selection favoured stability over windward performance.
sources.limit: Course angle and speed relative to wind not in the abstract.

sources.citation: Munro, C., Vue, Z., Behringer, R. R. and Dunn, C. W. (2019). Scientific Reports 9, 15522 (title not recorded here).
sources.access: Abstract and passages read by a verification agent.
sources.use: Physalia is a siphonophore that uses a gas-filled float as a sail; aeriform cells of the gas gland produce carbon monoxide.
sources.limit: Morphology and development of Physalia; passages only.
